Binance Impersonation Scam UK: Spot a Fake Message

Binance Verify can check whether a URL, email address, phone number, or social account is officially linked to Binance — use it before trusting a message.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-05 · Updated 2026-08-09 · 4 min read

Quick answer: A message warning your Binance account faces suspension unless you click a link is phishing designed to steal your login. Type binance.com yourself or use the official app, and check the message with Binance Verify. If you entered details, change your password from another device, enable two-factor authentication, and tell Report Fraud or Police Scotland on 101.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a Binance impersonation message looks like

This scam is an email, text, or direct message designed to look like it's from Binance, warning of suspicious login activity, a security hold, or account suspension. An example of the style: Unusual login detected on your Binance account. Verify your identity within 24 hours or your account will be permanently suspended. The message links to a fake Binance login page that captures your email and password the moment you enter them, giving the scammer direct access to your real account and any cryptocurrency in it.

Warning signs of a fake Binance message

  • It creates urgency: "immediate action required", "suspicious login detected", or a countdown to suspension.
  • The sender's address or the link's domain is close to, but not exactly, binance.com — small misspellings or extra words are the tell.
  • It arrives via social media DM, WhatsApp, or Telegram with account-security instructions you cannot verify inside your Binance account.
  • If you've set one up, the message does not include your personal anti-phishing code, or the code looks wrong.
  • You're asked to click a link to "verify", "unlock", or "reactivate" your account rather than being told to log in directly.
  • Someone offers to "recover" your account or funds for a fee after contacting you about a supposed problem — this is a follow-up scam.

How the scam works step by step

A message arrives claiming a problem with your Binance account, often urgent and threatening in tone. It contains a link to a page built to look identical to Binance's real login. You enter your email and password there, believing you're logging into your genuine account — the scammer now has those credentials and can log into your real Binance account immediately. If two-factor authentication isn't enabled, they can move any cryptocurrency held there straight to a wallet they control, usually within minutes, and often route it through several wallets afterwards to make tracing harder.

How to check a Binance message is genuine

Don't click the link. Open a browser and type binance.com directly, or use the official Binance app, and check your account and security notifications there — a genuine alert should be checkable inside your account, not only in a message. Use Binance Verify, Binance's own tool for checking whether a URL, email address, phone number, Telegram contact, or social account is officially linked to Binance, before acting on anything. If you've set up a personal anti-phishing code in your account settings, check that the message contains the correct code.

Binance also says it will never ask you to send funds or tokens through private communications. Report anything suspicious through Binance's in-app Support chat rather than replying to the message.

What to do if you've already entered your details

Change your Binance password immediately from a different, trusted device, and enable two-factor authentication if it isn't already on. Check your account's recent activity and withdrawal history for anything you don't recognise. If cryptocurrency has already left your account, report it to Binance Support straight away with the transaction details and wallet address — acting fast gives the best (though still limited) chance of a receiving exchange freezing funds before they move on. Change the password on any other account that shares the same email or password, starting with your email provider.

How to report a Binance impersonation scam in the UK

Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, including the message, sender details, and any wallet address involved. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Forward a phishing email to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk, or a text to 7726, and report the impersonation to Binance directly through in-app Support.

Frequently asked questions

Is Binance itself safe, or should I stop using it?

Binance is a real cryptocurrency exchange, but crypto is high risk and that does not make any message using Binance branding genuine. In the UK, the FCA's consumer warning, last updated in June 2023, says Binance Markets Limited is not permitted to undertake any regulated activity here and no other Binance Group entity holds any form of UK authorisation, registration or licence to conduct regulated activity. Check the FCA warning before relying on the platform. Access your account only by typing binance.com directly or via the official app, never through a link in an email, text, or DM, and keep two-factor authentication switched on.

How can I check whether a Binance email is genuine?

Use Binance Verify, the platform's own tool for checking whether a URL, email address, phone number, or social account is officially linked to Binance, and check whether the email contains the correct personal anti-phishing code if you've set one up. Never rely on how official a message looks alone.

I entered my Binance password on a fake site — what now?

Change your password immediately from a different device and turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't already active. Check your recent account activity, and if any cryptocurrency has already been moved, report it to Binance Support right away with the wallet address.

How do I report a Binance impersonation scam?

Report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland). Forward phishing emails to report@phishing.gov.uk, texts to 7726, and report the impersonation to Binance directly through in-app Support.

  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
